doc.title: Connections: reading a schema from the live database
doc.p: Every engine reads its schemas two ways: from files (a dump, definition files, table metadata) and from the live database, over a connection. This is the design for the live side, agreed before any code: what an engine provides, what the app shares across engines, how credentials are kept, and how a connection is set up and tested.

section.title: Profiles and secrets
section.p: A connection profile is a name, an engine, and the values of the fields that engine declares (host, port, user, database, TLS mode…). Profiles live in the workspace, and never hold a secret.
A secret (a password, a token) is kept in one of these, chosen per profile:

steps.item: the operating system's keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, the Linux secret service): the default when the secret is typed on the Connections page;
a file the database's own tools already use, by reference: ~/.my.cnf or a mysql_config_editor login path for MySQL, ~/.pgpass or a service file for PostgreSQL;
ambient credentials the database's cloud provides (gcloud application default credentials, an AWS profile), for the engines whose catalogs use them.

section.p: A secret is never written to the workspace, never logged, never put in a URL, never returned by the server's API and never seen by the agent. The server serves this machine only (it already refuses other hosts and origins).

section.title: The Connections page
section.p: One page in the canvas, shared by every engine, drawn from what each engine declares:

list.item: the list: each connection's name, engine, where it points (host and database, never the secret), when it was last tested and how that went;
adding or editing: choose the engine, and its form appears, built from the fields it declares (each with its label, kind, default and help); the secret field says where the secret will be kept;

Test: runs the engine's test and shows each step with what happened, so a failure says exactly where it failed: 1. reach: the host answers on the port; 2. secure: TLS as the profile asks (required, verified, or off), and the certificate; 3. sign in: the user and the secret are accepted; 4. version: the server's version, and the engine version a schema read from it will be designed for; 5. rights: the user can read the schema's definitions, and whether it can also change anything (a read-only user is recommended, and the test says so when it is not);
Read the schema: reads it into a new schema, or into an existing one to compare, with the same report a file import gives.

section.title: What an engine provides
section.p: A new optional part of the engine interface, Live:

list.item: its connection fields, as data: key, label, kind (text, number, one of a list, secret), default, help, required; so the Connections page and the agent's tools are built from them, and a new engine's connection form needs no canvas code;
test(profile, secret) -> steps: the five steps above, each passed or failed with what happened;

read(profile, secret, which) -> the schema and its report: read-only, every object the engine models, with the report adding up exactly as a file read's does; which names the databases (or namespaces) to read.

section.p: Every live read uses only statements that read. An engine reads the definitions the way its database writes them when it can (SHOW CREATE TABLE, SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE in MySQL), through the same reader its dumps go through, so a schema read live and one read from a dump of the same database are the same model.

section.title: The agent
section.p: The agent sees connection names, their engines and where they point, and can ask to read a schema from one; the server connects, with the secret it keeps. The agent never sees, sends or chooses a secret, and cannot create a profile; the person does that on the Connections page.

section.title: Reading a schema from its connection
section.p: A schema is tied to the saved connection it is read from and the database on it, with what it reads each time (decision read-scope): everything, or the parts (definitions only, with metadata, with usage), the kinds of object and the objects chosen. A read asks the server's version first and then only what that version has, as the engine declares it (decision version-facts); it reads gently, never inside the database it reads (decision gentle-read); it takes the server's usage when the server keeps it (decision usage-apart); and it reports every step for the read screen (decision read-screen). The connection test names the grants the server's version needs that the account lacks. The research behind it, measured on MySQL 5.7, 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7: live-mysql.xml.

list.item: Each engine's live part (its connection fields, its test, its live read, and the Live part of the interface the first engine needs) is built in that engine's own branch and pull request, with its dump reader: the MySQL engine first. The scoped read, its catalog sources and its usage are the task mysql live (t05, SF-121).

Connections in the app (profiles in the workspace, secrets in the keychain or referenced, the Connections page with its test, the agent's tools) is its own piece of work, built with the server and the canvas.
